# Bump charts {#sec-bump-charts}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
# fonts ----
library(extrafont)
library(sysfonts)
source("_common.R")
# use font
showtext::showtext_auto()
# set theme
ggplot2::theme_set(fmggp2::theme_visor(
    base_size = 13))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Theme: `theme_visor()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_visor()`, built from a green Handspring Visor Deluxe: a pale lavender background, a translucent green frame, a gray LCD panel, green, gray, mint, and silver marks, and a Trebuchet MS title.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggbump)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
set.seed(2000)
springboard_sales <- expand_grid(
  week = 1:12,
  module = c("Modem", "VisorPhone", "Games",
             "MP3 Player", "GPS", "Camera")) |>
  mutate(
    module = factor(module, levels = unique(module)),
    week_of = as.Date("2000-11-04") + 7 * (week - 1),
    avg_sales = case_when(
      module == "Modem" ~ 420 - 8 * (week - 1),
      module == "VisorPhone" ~ 300 + 15 * (week - 1),
      module == "Games" ~ 330,
      module == "MP3 Player" ~ 360 - 5 * (week - 1),
      module == "GPS" ~ 200 + 20 * (week - 1),
      module == "Camera" ~ 280 - 10 * (week - 1)),
    sales = rpois(n(), lambda = avg_sales)) |>
  group_by(week) |>
  mutate(rank = rank(-sales, ties.method = "random")) |>
  ungroup()
labs_bump <- labs(title = "Springboard module sales",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Weekly rank, winter 2000 to 2001",
  x = "Week of", y = "Rank",
  color = "Module")
ggp2_bump <- ggplot(springboard_sales,
    aes(x = week_of,
      y = rank,
      color = module)) +
    ggbump::geom_bump(linewidth = 2) +
    geom_text(data = filter(springboard_sales, week == 12),
      aes(label = module), color = "#3E3F3A",
      hjust = 0, nudge_x = 3) +
    scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.2))) +
    scale_y_reverse(breaks = 1:6) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("#50ADA0", "#21786B", "#808284",
                                  "#3E3F3A", "#B4BBAF", "#5CB8AC")) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

ggp2_bump +
  labs_bump
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a categorical variable**
:::

## Description

A bump chart shows how the order of groups changes over time.[^bump] Each group gets a line that goes up or down the `y` axis as its place in the order changes, and the lines run across all of the time on the `x` axis.[^bump-lines]

We can make bump charts in `ggplot2` with [`ggbump`](https://github.com/davidsjoberg/ggbump).[^ggbump]

## Set up


::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Bring in the code we'll use.[^packages]
:::


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_bump
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
# pak::pak("davidsjoberg/ggbump")
library(ggbump)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for data manipulation
library(tidyr) # for expand_grid()
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Handspring was a company that made small computers you could hold in one hand. It started selling the Visor, its first one, in 1999. The Springboard was an open space in the back of the Visor, and the Visor became whatever part you put in that space.[^springboard] By the end of 2000 there were parts for going on the Internet, playing games, playing music, finding where you are, and taking pictures, and the new VisorPhone, which turned the Visor into a phone.[^modules] We'll make up[^simulate] 12 weeks of sales for six Springboard parts (how many of each part sold across a group of stores).[^units] Each part gets a mean for each week (`avg_sales`) that goes up, goes down, or stays the same, and `rpois()` picks each week's sales close to that mean.[^rpois] Then we put the parts in order within each week (`rank`), with `1` for the part that sold the most. Starting with `set.seed()`[^seed] means you'll get the same 72 rows every time you run the code below.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_bump
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(2000) # same 12 weeks of sales every time the code runs
springboard_sales <- expand_grid(
  week = 1:12, # 12 weeks of sales
  module = c("Modem", "VisorPhone", "Games", # six Springboard modules
             "MP3 Player", "GPS", "Camera") # (every module appears in every week)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    module = factor(module, levels = unique(module)), # keep modules in the order above
    week_of = as.Date("2000-11-04") + 7 * (week - 1), # first day of each week
    avg_sales = case_when( # average weekly sales for each module
      module == "Modem" ~ 420 - 8 * (week - 1), # starts on top, then slowly falls
      module == "VisorPhone" ~ 300 + 15 * (week - 1), # climbs each week
      module == "Games" ~ 330, # holds steady
      module == "MP3 Player" ~ 360 - 5 * (week - 1), # slowly falls
      module == "GPS" ~ 200 + 20 * (week - 1), # starts last, climbs fastest
      module == "Camera" ~ 280 - 10 * (week - 1) # falls each week
      ),
    sales = rpois(n(), lambda = avg_sales) # weekly sales counts around each average
    ) |>
  group_by(week) |> # rank the modules within each week
  mutate(
    rank = rank(-sales, ties.method = "random") # 1 = best seller (ties broken at random)
    ) |>
  ungroup()
glimpse(springboard_sales)
```
:::

## Distribution

A bump chart leaves out the sales and keeps only the order. That makes it easy to see which part went past which, but it also doesn't show *how close* the race was. When two parts sell about the same number, chance alone can make them trade places from one week to the next, even though nothing real changed.[^noise] Below we'll move from the sales, to a graph, to the rule behind it.[^formula]

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first week.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_bump
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
springboard_sales |>
  filter(week == 1) |>
  select(module, avg_sales, sales, rank) |>
  arrange(rank)
```
:::

Every part sold close to its mean (no more than about 30 over or under), and the order of the parts is the same as the order of their means. Below we find how many times each part changed places from one week to the next.[^rank-changes]

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_bump
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
rank_changes <- springboard_sales |>
  group_by(module) |>
  summarise(rank_changes = sum(rank != lag(rank), na.rm = TRUE),
            first_rank = first(rank), last_rank = last(rank))
rank_changes
```
:::

The VisorPhone and GPS go up because their means go up, and the Modem and Camera go down because their means go down. But Games changes places `r rank_changes$rank_changes[rank_changes$module == "Games"]` times, even though its mean never changes.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

The graph below shows the sales for Games and the MP3 Player. The band of color around each line reaches above and below the mean by two times how far sales usually fall from the mean (more on that below).[^ribbon] Where the two bands cover each other, either part could come out ahead in that week.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_bump
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
two_modules <- springboard_sales |>
  filter(module %in% c("Games", "MP3 Player"))
ggplot(two_modules, aes(x = week_of, color = module, fill = module)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = avg_sales - 2 * sqrt(avg_sales),
                  ymax = avg_sales + 2 * sqrt(avg_sales)),
              alpha = 1 / 4, color = NA) +
  geom_line(aes(y = sales), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = sales), size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Games" = "#808284", "MP3 Player" = "#21786B"),
                     aesthetics = c("color", "fill")) +
  labs(title = "Games and MP3 Player sales",
       subtitle = "Bands show each week's mean plus or minus 2 SD",
       caption = "Simulated data",
       x = "Week of", y = "Units sold", color = "Module", fill = "Module")
```
:::

The bands cover each other in all 12 weeks, which is why these two parts change places in the bump chart.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

The sales for each part in each week come from [a rule for how many times something happens at a set rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution),[^poisson] with its own mean for that week ($\lambda$):

$$
\text{sales}_{m,w} \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_{m,w})
$$

For the number of times something happens at a set rate, how far that number usually falls from the mean is $\sqrt{\lambda}$,[^sd] so the sales of a part with a mean of 330 move up and down by about $\sqrt{330} \approx 18$ a week (the bands above reach two times that, about 36, above and below the mean). A hill is a line that is high in the middle and low on both sides. The difference between the sales of two parts falls close to a hill,[^normal] with a mean of $\lambda_1 - \lambda_2$, and it usually falls $\sqrt{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}$ from that mean.[^gap-sd] In week one, the mean for the MP3 Player is 360 and the mean for Games is 330, so the chance that Games comes out ahead anyway is:

$$
P(\text{swap}) \approx \Phi\left(\frac{-(360 - 330)}{\sqrt{360 + 330}}\right) \approx `r round(pnorm(-30 / sqrt(690)), 2)`
$$

By week seven, both parts have a mean of 330, and the chance is one in two (0.5). Charts of order are great for showing which part is on top, but when two parts are close, a change in their order is often just chance.[^poisson-noise] Try making the means two times as far from each other in `case_when()`, and the bump chart moves around a lot less.

## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::

  - Make the words around the graph[^labels] with `labs()`

  - Put `week_of` on the `x` axis and `rank` on the `y` axis, and give each `module` its own color[^aes]

  - Add `ggbump::geom_bump()` and set `linewidth` to `2`

  - Put the `y` axis the other way up with `scale_y_reverse()` so place `1` is on top[^reverse]

  - Pick six line colors with `scale_color_manual()` (the look only has four)[^palette]

  - Write the name of each part at the end of its line with `geom_text()`, and make room for the names with `scale_x_date()`

  - Take away the list of colors with `theme(legend.position = "none")`[^legend]

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_bump
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
labs_bump <- labs(title = "Springboard module sales",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Weekly rank, winter 2000 to 2001",
  x = "Week of", y = "Rank",
  color = "Module")
ggp2_bump <- ggplot(springboard_sales,
    aes(x = week_of,
      y = rank,
      color = module)) +
    ggbump::geom_bump(linewidth = 2) +
    geom_text(data = filter(springboard_sales, week == 12),
      aes(label = module), color = "#3E3F3A",
      hjust = 0, nudge_x = 3) +
    scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.2))) +
    scale_y_reverse(breaks = 1:6) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("#50ADA0", "#21786B", "#808284",
                                  "#3E3F3A", "#B4BBAF", "#5CB8AC")) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

ggp2_bump +
  labs_bump
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_bump
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_bump <- labs(title = "Springboard module sales",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Weekly rank, winter 2000 to 2001",
  x = "Week of", y = "Rank",
  color = "Module")
ggp2_bump <- ggplot(springboard_sales,
    aes(x = week_of,
      y = rank,
      color = module)) +
    ggbump::geom_bump(linewidth = 2) +
    geom_text(data = filter(springboard_sales, week == 12),
      aes(label = module), color = "#3E3F3A",
      hjust = 0, nudge_x = 3) +
    scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.2))) +
    scale_y_reverse(breaks = 1:6) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("#50ADA0", "#21786B", "#808284",
                                  "#3E3F3A", "#B4BBAF", "#5CB8AC")) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

ggp2_bump +
  labs_bump
```

[^bump]: Bump charts show how numerical (ranked) values change over time for different categories (or groups).

[^bump-lines]: Differences are represented with connecting lines (along the `y` axis) that cover the full timescale (along the `x` axis).

[^ggbump]: The `ggbump` package.

[^packages]: Install and load the packages.

[^springboard]: The Springboard expansion slot on the back of the handheld turned it into whatever module you slid in.

[^modules]: A modem, a games cartridge, an MP3 player, a GPS receiver, a camera, and the VisorPhone (which turned the Visor into a cell phone).

[^simulate]: Simulate.

[^units]: Module sales: the number of units sold across a panel of retailers.

[^rpois]: `rpois()` draws each week's actual sales from a Poisson distribution with `lambda = avg_sales`.

[^seed]: Setting the random seed. Each row is one module week (12 weeks × 6 modules).

[^noise]: Random week to week noise can swap their ranks.

[^formula]: The formula.

[^rank-changes]: Rank changes: the weeks where a module's rank is different from the week before.

[^ribbon]: The ribbon covers the average plus or minus two standard deviations ($\lambda \pm 2\sqrt{\lambda}$).

[^poisson]: A Poisson distribution.

[^sd]: A Poisson count has a standard deviation of $\sqrt{\lambda}$.

[^normal]: The gap between two modules is approximately normal.

[^gap-sd]: A standard deviation of $\sqrt{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}$.

[^poisson-noise]: Small gaps between ranks are often just Poisson noise.

[^labels]: Labels.

[^aes]: Map `week_of` to `x`, `rank` to `y`, and `module` to `color`.

[^reverse]: Reverse the `y` scale so rank `1` is at the top.

[^palette]: The theme's discrete palette only has four colors.

[^legend]: The legend.
